fields.complete_source:
Solution
(1) **Uniqueness of bipartition in a connected bipartite graph.** **Proof:** Let G be a connected
bipartite graph, so V (G) can be split into two parts (A, B) such that every edge joins a vertex in
A to a vertex in B. We claim this bipartition is essentially unique (the only possible bipartition is
(A, B) up to swapping A and B).
Indeed, pick an arbitrary vertex v0 ∈V (G). Because G is connected, every other vertex x ∈V (G)
can be reached by some path from v0. In any bipartition of G, the **parity** of the length of
a path from v0 to x determines on which side of the partition x must lie: if the shortest path
from v0 to x has even length, then x must be in the same part as v0; if the shortest path has odd
length, then x must lie in the opposite part. (This follows because edges connect opposite parts,
so each step along a path alternates the side of the bipartition.) Moreover, in a bipartite graph
any two distinct paths between the same vertices have the **same parity** of length (otherwise
combining an even-length and an odd-length path would produce an odd cycle, which cannot occur
in a bipartite graph). Thus the parity of the distance from v0 to x is well-defined and independent
of the chosen path.
Therefore, starting with v0 in part A, we are forced to place every vertex at even distance from v0
into A and every vertex at odd distance into B. This yields a unique 2-coloring (bipartition) of G.
Any other bipartition of G **must** assign v0 to one of the two parts; if it assigns v0 to A, then
by the same reasoning every neighbor of v0 must lie in the opposite part B, every distance-2 vertex
in A, etc., reproducing the same division (A, B). If instead v0 were assigned to the other part in
some coloring, that coloring is just the “swapped” partition (B, A). Hence no different bipartition
exists. In summary, for a connected bipartite graph the division of V (G) into two independent sets
is unique up to relabeling of the two parts.
□
(2) **Non-bipartite graphs contain an induced odd cycle.** **Proof:** Suppose G is *not* bipartite.
We must show G has an **odd-length cycle** (circuit) that is an *induced* subgraph of G.
First, we prove that G contains *some* cycle of odd length. A standard approach is via a contradic-
tion to 2-colorability: try to color each vertex either Red or Blue so that every edge has differently
colored endpoints. Because G is not bipartite, no such proper 2-coloring exists. Start by choosing
an arbitrary vertex v and color it Red. Then color its neighbors Blue, the next neighbors Red, and
so on (for example, perform a breadth-first search coloring by distance from v). This process will
eventually encounter a conflict: at some stage there will be an edge {x, y} such that x and y were
colored the same color. Let x and y be the first such pair encountered. By construction, x and
y have the same “distance” (level) from the start vertex v (since otherwise one would have been
colored earlier than the other). Let Px be the shortest path from v to x in the BFS tree, and Py
the shortest path from v to y. These v–x and v–y paths each have the same length, say ℓedges
(and ℓis even, because x and y ended up the same color). Now consider the closed walk obtained
by following Px from v to x, then the edge {x, y}, then Py in reverse from y back to v. This is
a cycle in G. The length of this cycle is ℓ(from v to x) + 1 (edge x–y) + ℓ(from y back to v)
= 2ℓ+ 1, which is **odd**. Thus G does contain an odd-length cycle.
Now let C be a cycle of odd length in G, and assume C is chosen to be as short as possible (i.e. C
is a *shortest* odd cycle in G). Suppose, for sake of contradiction, that C is **not** an induced
subgraph. Then C has a *chord*: an edge connecting two vertices of C that is not itself one of
the cycle edges. Let the vertices of C in cyclic order be v1, v2, . . . , v2k+1 (with 2k + 1 odd). If
there is a chord between some vi and vj (with j ̸= i ± 1), that chord together with the edges of C
between vi and vj forms a smaller cycle. In fact, the chord vivj splits the original cycle into two
cycles: one cycle C1 goes from vi to vj along the original cycle C and then directly back to vi along
the chord vivj, and the other cycle C2 goes the opposite way around C from vi to vj and returns
via the chord. Both C1 and C2 are strictly shorter than C (since the chord provides a shortcut).
1

Moreover, at least one of C1 or C2 has **odd** length: because C had odd length, the two new
cycles C1, C2 cannot both be even (intuitively, an odd number cannot be written as the sum of two
even numbers). To see this formally, write |C| = 2k + 1 and suppose the path from vi to vj along
C consists of m edges. Then the complementary path has length (2k + 1) −m edges. Including
the chord, the two new cycles have lengths m + 1 and ((2k + 1) −m) + 1 = 2k + 2 −m. One of m
or 2k + 1 −m is even (since their sum 2k + 1 is odd), so one of m + 1 or 2k + 2 −m is odd. Thus
one of C1, C2 is an odd-length cycle. But this contradicts the assumption that C was the shortest
odd cycle in G. Therefore C cannot have any chord. This means that no two non-adjacent vertices
of C are connected by an edge in G. Equivalently, the subgraph of G induced by the vertices
{v1, v2, . . . , v2k+1} has exactly the edges of the cycle C and no others. In other words, C is an
**induced** odd cycle in G, as required.
□
(3) **Characterization of bipartite graphs via edge cuts.** **Claim:** An undirected graph G is
bipartite if and only if its edge set E(G) can be partitioned into one or more **cuts**.
(Here a *cut* means the set of all edges between a chosen subset S ⊆V (G) and its complement
V (G) \ S.)
**Proof:** “⇒” If G is bipartite, let (U, W) be its bipartition (so U ∪W = V (G), U ∩W = ∅, and
every edge joins U to W). Then **all** edges of G go between U and W. In particular, the entire
edge set E(G) itself is the cut determined by S = U (since the edges between U and V (G)\U = W
are exactly the edges of G). Thus E(G) can be “partitioned” into a single cut. (A single set {E(G)}
is a valid partition of E(G).) This establishes the forward direction.
“⇐” Now assume E(G) can be partitioned into a collection of cut sets. That is, suppose there exist
subsets S1, S2, . . . , Sk ⊆V (G) such that each part Ei of the partition is Ei = { uv ∈E(G) : u ∈
Si, v ∈V (G) \ Si }. Each Ei is a cut in G, and {E1, . . . , Ek} is a partition of E(G) (so the Ei are
disjoint and E1 ∪· · · ∪Ek = E(G)).
We will show that under this assumption G has no cycle of odd length. That will imply G is
bipartite (since a graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no odd cycle). Consider any cycle C
in G. Let its edges be e1, e2, . . . , en in cyclic order (with n = |C|). Each edge ej belongs to exactly
one of the cut sets Ei. Moreover, if ej ∈Ei, that means one endpoint of ej lies in Si and the other
lies in V (G) \ Si. In terms of *vertex coloring*, we can associate to each cut Ei a 2-coloring of
G (color vertices “0” if they lie in Si, and “1” if they lie in V (G) \ Si). Then ej ∈Ei implies that
in the i-th coloring, the endpoints of ej have opposite colors (“0–1” or “1–0”). If instead ej /∈Ei,
then both endpoints of ej lie on the same side of the cut Si – meaning in the i-th coloring, ej’s
endpoints have the **same** color.
Now, traverse the cycle C = v1v2 · · · vnv1. For each cut Ei, track the parity of how many edges
of C belong to Ei. As we go around C, every time we traverse an edge from Ei we “flip” between
color 0 and color 1 under the i-th coloring; if we traverse an edge not in Ei, the i-color does not
change. Since v1 starts and ends at the same vertex, by the time we return to v1 we must come
back to the original color (0 or 1) in the i-th coloring. Therefore, the total number of edges of C
that lie in Ei must be **even** (an odd number of flips would change the color). This argument
holds for each i = 1, 2, . . . , k. Let mi be the number of edges of the cycle C that belong to Ei.
We have just established mi is even for each i. On the other hand, since {E1, . . . , Ek} partition all
edges, every edge of C lies in exactly one Ei. So m1 + m2 + · · · + mk = n (the length of the cycle).
But the sum of even integers mi is even, so n must be even. Thus **every** cycle in G has even
length; no odd cycle exists in G.
Finally, a graph with no odd cycles is necessarily bipartite (this is a well-known characterization,
but we outline the reasoning: Without odd cycles, we can 2-color each connected component of
G by a simple breadth-first search from an arbitrary start vertex, coloring alternating layers red
and blue. Any conflict in this coloring would produce an odd cycle, which cannot happen. Thus a
proper 2-coloring exists, proving the graph is bipartite). Therefore G is bipartite.
□
2

fields.flaw: In part (2), the proof claims that the closed walk formed by the BFS-tree path Px from v to x, the conflict edge {x,y}, and the reversed BFS-tree path Py from y to v is a cycle in G of length 2ℓ+1. This is false in general: the two BFS-tree paths can share internal vertices, so the concatenation is only a closed odd walk, not a cycle, and G need not contain any cycle of length 2ℓ+1. (A second, independent local claim in the same paragraph — "This process will eventually encounter a conflict" when starting BFS from an arbitrary vertex — is also refutable by a disconnected witness.)
fields.problem:
Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 35
Prove the following properties regarding undirected graphs: (1) Prove that if a bipartite
graph is connected, its bipartition is unique. (2) Prove that every non-bipartite graph
possesses an odd circuit as an induced subgraph. (3) Prove that an undirected graph G
is bipartite if and only if its edge set E(G) admits a partition into cuts.
1

fields.witness:
PRIMARY (target sentence "This is a cycle in G"): G = triangle with a pendant vertex. V(G) = {0,1,2,3}, E(G) = {{0,1},{0,2},{0,3},{1,2}}. G is connected and non-bipartite. Run BFS from v = 3: levels are L(3)=0, L(0)=1, L(1)=2, L(2)=2. The edge {x,y} = {1,2} is a conflict edge (both endpoints at level l = 2). The BFS-tree paths are forced (unique, independent of tie-breaking): Px = 3,0,1 and Py = 3,0,2. They share the INTERNAL vertex 0. The concatenation Px . {1,2} . reverse(Py) = 3,0,1,2,0,3 is a closed walk with 5 = 2l+1 edges, but vertex 0 occurs twice, so it is NOT a cycle. Moreover the exact set of simple-cycle lengths present in G is {3}: claim says G contains a cycle of length 2l+1 = 5; here the cycle lengths of G are {3}, and 5 is not among them (G has only 4 vertices, so no 5-cycle can exist under ANY choice of BFS tree or tie-breaking order).

SECONDARY ("This process will eventually encounter a conflict"): G = triangle {0,1,2} plus isolated vertex 3, i.e. V = {0,1,2,3}, E = {{0,1},{0,2},{1,2}}. G is non-bipartite (odd cycle length 3). BFS started at v = 3 reaches only {3}; the number of edges with both endpoints reached and at equal level is 0. Claim says a conflict is eventually encountered; here zero conflicts are ever encountered although G is non-bipartite.

Both witnesses are the minimum-size ones (by |V| then |E|) over the whole searched space.
